candidates.title: Normalize-Then-Precondition: A Hierarchical Approach to Marginal Scale and Interaction Geometry for LLM Training
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Matrix optimizers have emerged as a promising direction, with Muon standing out as a prominent design. Revisiting Muon through its full-Gram representation, we observe that it jointly processes marginal-scale and interaction information. This opens an alternative way to organize geometric information hierarchically, motivating the Normalize-Then-Precondition framework. Specifically, it first uses diagonal-Gram information to construct a marginally normalized update, then applies spectral preconditioning to its directional interaction geometry. Building on this framework, we develop NormPre with NormPre-G and NormPre-L adopting global and localized spectral preconditioning, grounded in spectral-norm steepest descent and a regularized formulation followed by leading mode selection, respectively. To enable large-scale training, NormPre-G uses Newton-Schulz iterations and NormPre-L employs randomized sketching to approximate the leading interaction eigenspace. Theoretically, we establish $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2})$ convergence guarantees for simplified versions of NormPre. candidates.abstract_excerpt: We propose a novel optimizer for low-rank adaptation (LoRA) that explicitly incorporates the gauge symmetry of low-rank factorization. Our optimizer extends recent matrix optimizers for full-parameter training to the manifold of fixed-rank matrices by interpreting them as normalization under a rotated basis. We show how rotation and normalization can be integrated with the fixed-rank manifold efficiently. Our optimizer converges faster to lower held-out loss and achieves better or comparable downstream performance on both supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks.

candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a widely used approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), yet a performance gap can remain relative to full fine-tuning (FFT). Many LoRA variants improve the initialization or optimization of low-rank factors. At each training step, however, their first-order weight-space directions are constrained by the current parameterization. We characterize the corresponding LoRA-accessible gradient space and show that it coincides with the tangent space induced by the current LoRA parameterization. This characterization yields an orthogonal decomposition of the full weight gradient at the current model parameters. We term the component orthogonal to this space the normal gradient. candidates.title: Scaling Repeated-Data Pretraining: Batch Size, Regularization, and GPU-Time Tradeoffs
candidates.abstract_excerpt: We study pretraining when compute is abundant but unique training data are finite, requiring repeated training on the same data. We first revisit infinite-compute pretraining (Kim et al. 2026) and show that its frontier depends critically on choices previously fixed or studied only in isolation. In particular, optimizing batch size together with epoch counts reveals a U-shaped relationship between validation loss and batch size, favoring smaller batches than typical pretraining, likely because small-batch gradient noise provides implicit regularization. We further find that training recipes, previously optimized under a single-pass assumption, can be tuned, e.g., repacking documents into new sequences every epoch, weight tying, and positive embedding weight decay. We then relax the infinite-compute assumption. In particular, smaller-than-typical batch sizes can require prohibitively long sequential training, motivating to treat GPUs and time as separate resources. candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is now a standard approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks. This covariance determines which low-rank perturbations are statistically observable. candidates.title: First-Order LoRA Training with Phone NPUs
candidates.abstract_excerpt: On-device fine-tuning lets a large language model (LLM) learn from its user's private data without uploading it. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces the trainable parameters, but each first-order training step still multiplies by the frozen base-model weights during the forward pass, activation recomputation, and input-gradient computation. candidates.title: Robust Parameter-Efficient LLM Adaptation on Analog Hardware
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Analog in-memory computing is a promising platform for on-device execution of large language models because it performs matrix--vector multiplications (MVMs) in memory and in parallel, reducing data movement. However, limited digital-to-analog converter precision, input noise, and finite conductance states can degrade model accuracy, while full-model retraining to address these effects can be costly. We develop an optimizer-agnostic, parameter-efficient adaptation method based on Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), keeping the pretrained weights stored on analog arrays fixed while training the LoRA weights to adapt to downstream tasks and hardware non-idealities. Reliable adaptation requires handling errors in both forward and backward MVMs and physical weight updates. We use input reshaping to reduce input-induced MVM errors and update accumulation to retain small updates before programming them to finite-state analog devices. Across Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct and Llama-3-8B with both Muon and AdamW, input reshaping improves analog LoRA fine-tuning under noisy MVM computation. candidates.title: BMuon: Budgeting Muon's Spectral Geometry for Structured Compressibility
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. The resulting oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under a family of norms that interpolate between Muon's geometry and structured sparse geometries. Our principal sparsity control is an interpretable global channel-allocation budget, rather than a setting-dependent sparsity-penalty coefficient. candidates.title: A Fine-Grained Analysis of the LoRA Fine-Tuning Landscape with Implications for Data Selection
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a standard approach for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, yet a fundamental practical question remains unresolved: how should the adapter rank be chosen? An overly small rank may lead to a poorly conditioned optimization landscape, whereas an unnecessarily large rank sacrifices the efficiency that motivates LoRA in the first place. Existing theoretical analyses provide only limited guidance on this trade-off, and their guarantees are typically established under restrictive theoretical settings. We address this gap by developing a substantially sharper landscape theory for LoRA, building on modern results from nonconvex low-rank matrix sensing. candidates.title: FedLore: Communication and Memory Efficient Federated Learning via Shared Gradient Low-Rank Projection
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Federated training of foundation models is constrained by client memory and communication costs. LoRA-based methods reduce these costs through low-rank adapters, but their fixed rank budget can limit adaptation. The shared basis enables exact aggregation in low-rank coordinates and eliminates the identified projection bias. Subspace refresh allows the accumulated model update to exceed the per-round rank budget. candidates.title: Stochastic Projections and Rank-Aware Learning Rates for Federated LoRA
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Fine-tuning large-scale foundation models across resource-constrained, distributed clients presents significant computational and communication challenges. candidates.title: LoGRA: Scaling LLM Reinforcement Learning with Low-Rank Gradient Sketches
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Reinforcement learning has greatly advanced the capabilities of large language models, but its memory demands remain a barrier to broader adoption. We introduce LoGRA, an approach to RL post-training that reduces memory by retaining useful learning signals in low-rank gradient sketches. These compact representations support both model updates and efficient policy synchronization. To prevent overly large updates from disrupting learning, we complement gradient compression with predicted-KL step control, which estimates policy changes before applying each update and adjusts its magnitude accordingly. With all techniques combined, LoGRA reduces average training memory usage by up to 45.7% across reasoning tasks without compromising performance. It also enables stable training of a 27B-parameter model for over 1,100 steps on a single eight-GPU node, where dense Adam runs out of memory, making previously memory-infeasible RL training practical. candidates.title: DT-LoRA: Reaching Beyond the Tangent Space of Low-Rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning. We investigate this performance gap through a tangent-space lens: factorized updates are confined to the tangent space of the current low-rank factors, leaving gradient components outside this space unexploited. candidates.title: Low-rank Low Precision Training of Gaussian Processes
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Training Gaussian processes (GPs) at large scale is computationally challenging because evaluating the log-marginal likelihood and its gradients involves large, dense kernel matrices. candidates.title: Ori: Drift-Aware Streaming $k$-PCA for Very Low-Rank LLM Training
candidates.abstract_excerpt: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. Ori employs a streaming $k$-PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. candidates.title: A Margin Perspective on LoRA: Robustness to Catastrophic Forgetting and Adapter Merging (MaLoRA)
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the de facto method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks, achieving strong task adaptation with minimal trainable parameters and low optimization cost. candidates.title: When and How Does Muon Precondition? The Role of Structured Gradient Noise
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Muon has become a popular optimizer for large language model training, yet its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. In this work, we study how gradient noise geometry shapes Muon's preconditioning benefits. We first show, theoretically and empirically, that under the classical isotropic noise assumption, Muon offers no acceleration beyond a rescaling of the learning rate. This motivates us to investigate structured noise arising from mini-batch sampling in associative memory with heterogeneous task frequencies. We establish an exact balancing threshold for two tasks and extend the analysis to multiple tasks, revealing how task coverage and gradient reliability jointly shape learning. 2610.22794:1a6de093f1889870c20181b7c12b2.question: In the 1B LLaMA pretraining experiments, what are Ori's measured peak GPU memory, training throughput or wall-clock cost, and validation loss or perplexity compared with GaLore-style low-rank optimizers and full-rank baselines at matched rank and training budget?

passages.text: Figure 1 : Trade-off between evaluation perplexity (Y-axis, lower is better) and peak optimizer state memory (X-axis, lower is better) for various low-rank optimizers in different ranks on the 1B LLaMA pre-training task. Bottom-left corner is the ideal region. Ori ( ⋆ \star ) forms a better Pareto frontier, achieving a superior performance-to-memory trade-off compared to state-of-the-art baselines like GaLore ( ∘ \circ ) and OSD ( □ \square ). However, existing adaptation strategies may overlook a key empirical observation that we make explicit in this work: the gradient subspace does not jump erratically but, rather, drifts smoothly after warm-up. In other words, the projector at step t t is predictably close to that at t − Δ ​ t t-\Delta t for small Δ ​ t \Delta t (e.g., 20). This slow, structured drift suggests a different perspective. Rather than recomputing the subspace (as in GaLore [ 39 ] ) or optimizing it with non-convex gradient descent (as in OSD [ 15 ] ), we can track it with a streaming update that makes small, frequent rotations aligned with the most recent gradients, while also preserving and transferring optimizer statistics across these rotations. In light of these observations, we arrive at a different design problem: How do we continuously maintain a memory-light, compute-efficient, and stable projector that tracks a drifting gradient subspace?

We evaluate Ori’s pre-training performance against the baselines on the C4 dataset [ 26 ] using LLaMA-architecture models of four sizes (60M, 130M, 350M, and 1B), following similar experimental settings as prior work [ 14 , 39 ] . Departing from prior work that often tests a single rank, we systematically evaluate all low-rank methods across three distinct ranks for each model (e.g., r ∈ { 512,128 , 32 } r\in\{512,128,32\} for the 1B model), enabling a rigorous assessment of optimizer performance under varying degrees of memory constraints. To ensure a fair comparison, model hyperparameters were held constant for each model size, while each optimizer’s learning rate was tuned from { 0.01 , 0.005 , 0.001 , 0.0005 , 0.0001 } \{0.01,0.005,0.001,0.0005,0.0001\} . We report validation perplexity after a fixed token budget, with full details provided in Appendix E .

As shown in Table 1 , Ori’s performance is consistently strong, particularly in memory-constrained scenarios. At higher, less restrictive ranks (e.g., r = 128 r=128 for the 60M model, r = 256 r=256 for the 130M model), Ori performs on par with GaLore, establishing it as a highly competitive method in common low-rank settings. However, Ori’s distinct advantage emerges when the rank r r is severely constrained, where it demonstrates the most robust performance as its accuracy degrades the least under memory pressure. This trend, where the cost of a stale subspace projection becomes most apparent, is consistent across all model scales. For instance, when training the 130M model at an aggressively low rank of just 16, Ori achieves a validation perplexity of 43.61, substantially outperforming GaLore (60.29) and OSD (54.05). This result empirically validates our central hypothesis: actively tracking the gradient subspace drift is most critical when the optimizer has the fewest dimensions to work with. By excelling in these challenging low-rank regimes, Ori consistently narrows the performance gap to full-rank Adam, pushing the performance boundaries of memory-efficient optimization.

We profile the optimizer state peak memory and wall-clock time during the pre-training experiments from Section 5.2 . Details on the memory profiling procedure can be found in Section E.8 . As shown in Table 9 , Ori exhibits a superior efficiency profile among standard, non-error-feedback gradient-subspace methods (Adam, ReLoRA, GaLore, OSD). In addition, as shown in Table 10 , O-LDAdam demonstrates competitive and comparable efficiency profile to the error-feedback baseline LDAdam under the large update frequency regime ( T = 200 T=200 ). Full table on pre-training of other model sizes can be found in Appendix F . Memory Usage: Compared to standard, non-error-feedback baselines, Ori consistently consumes the least optimizer peak memory across all ranks. For instance, at rank 32, Ori requires only 0.2487 GB, which is 12.1% less than OSD (0.2832 GB) and 26.5% less than GaLore (0.3385 GB). This confirms Ori’s tangible memory savings. On the other hand, compared to the error-feedback methods, O-LDAdam consistently yields the same memory footprint as LDAdam baselines. Training Speed: Despite updating its subspace projector 10x more frequently ( T Ori = 20 T_{\text{Ori}}=20 vs. T GaLore/OSD = 200 T_{\text{GaLore/OSD}}=200 ), Ori is still the fastest among all standard, non-error-feedback methods. While the weight-subspace method ReLoRA is faster at lower ranks due to its different update mechanism, its worse model performance (see Table 1 ) highlights a clear trade-off. In contrast, Ori achieves superior model performance without compromising on speed, making it a more effective and efficient choice overall. The lightweight nature of the Oja++ update allows Ori to be both more accurate and faster than its direct competitors, making it a better choice for efficient training.

On the other hand, although O-LDAdam yields a slightly longer average update time than LDAdam with T = 200 T=200 due to the need to perform power iterations multiple times ( Algorithm 3 ), the additional cost is not prohibitively large. Moreover, O-LDAdam demonstrates a nontrivial speedup compared to the standard LDAdam setting with a per-step update schedule ( T = 1 T=1 ). Together with the model performance results shown in Table 2 , this demonstrates that O-LDAdam strikes a good balance between model performance and computational cost in the extremely low-rank regime. Table 11 presents the full results of memory and Wallclock time comparison of all the optimizer methods on the LLaMA model pre-training task on the C4 dataset. As shown by the table, our method Ori achieves superior memory and computation time profile almost across the broad, demonstrating its general efficiency under various settings. Table 11 : Memory and Wallclock Time Comparison of pre-training various sized LLaMa model on the C4 dataset.

2610.11730:fcb9657504cda6ec5a5ce705df0a5.question: In the LLaMA 124M–500M experiments, how were spectral weight decay and standard weight decay matched on validation loss and training budget, and what were the measured training-memory, throughput, or compute overheads and SVD-LLM compression results?

passages.text: BRAIn Lab Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights Dmitrii Andriianov 1 , Andrey Veprikov 1,2 , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1,3 1 Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) 2 SB AI Lab 3 Innopolis University Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SpectralWD .

To make the regularizer matrix-aware, we begin with the proximal interpretation of decoupled weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and a 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. At 60 % 60\% label noise, mean clean-test accuracy gains over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization reach 17.78 17.78 points on MNIST and 4.59 4.59 points on four BERT-base tasks.

Spectral weight decay lowers the effective rank of weight matrices, making them amenable to low-rank compression. We use SVD-LLM [ Wang et al., 2024 ] , which gives the lowest validation loss in our matched comparison. We compress each weight matrix to its own effective rank, which varies substantially across layers (Figure 2 , middle). We leave the token embeddings and output head uncompressed because their ranks respond little to spectral weight decay, and compressing them even to their effective ranks sharply degrades model quality. The comparison and compression procedure are described in Appendix B.4 . Figure 3 (top) reports the maximum compression rate supported by each validation-loss distortion budget. Spectral weight decay substantially shifts this frontier upward at all three model scales. For the 500 500 M model and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it supports 1.89 × 1.89\times compression, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times after standard weight decay. The same factorization reduces the FLOPs of a linear layer when r ⁡ ( m + n ) < m ​ n r(m+n)<mn . This reduction does not translate directly into lower latency because the factorized forward pass evaluates ( U r ​ Σ r ) ​ ( V r ⊤ ​ X ) (U_{r}\Sigma_{r})(V_{r}^{\top}X) with two GEMMs instead of the single GEMM W ​ X WX . The additional kernel launch and intermediate activation can offset the reduction in FLOPs. To improve tensor-core utilization, we round the effective rank down to the nearest multiple of 16 16 , r l = max ⁡ ( 16 , 16 ​ ⌊ erank ⁡ ( W l ) 16 ⌋ ) , r_{l}=\max\!\left(16,\,16\left\lfloor\frac{\operatorname{erank}(W_{l})}{16}\right\rfloor\right), (3)

The compression results in Section 3 use SVD-LLM. We compare five singular-value-based compression methods on one checkpoint to select this method. Table 2 applies truncated SVD, SliceGPT [ Ashkboos et al., 2024 ] , ASVD [ Yuan et al., 2023 ] , SVD-LLM [ Wang et al., 2024 ] , and Dobi-SVD [ Wang et al., 2025 ] to a 124 124 M-parameter spectral-weight-decay model with coefficient 1 1 . We also report accuracy on ARC-Easy [ Clark et al., 2018 ] , HellaSwag [ Zellers et al., 2019 ] , and PIQA [ Bisk et al., 2020 ] after compression. Truncated SVD reaches 1.43 × 1.43\times compression with a + 0.0359 +0.0359 validation-loss increase. SliceGPT produces a larger loss increase at a lower compression rate. ASVD and SVD-LLM preserve validation loss better at comparable compression, with increases of + 0.0286 +0.0286 and + 0.0196 +0.0196 , respectively. Dobi-SVD reaches a similar + 0.0207 +0.0207 increase at 1.21 × 1.21\times compression. SVD-LLM gives the lowest validation loss among the compressed models, so we use it throughout. Spectral weight decay also has little effect on their ranks (Figure 2 , left). We choose a separate truncation rank for each remaining weight matrix because effective rank varies substantially across transformer blocks (Figure 2 , middle). After folding the singular values into one factor, a rank- r r approximation of W ∈ ℝ m × n W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} stores r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) parameters instead of m ​ n mn . Decreasing r r therefore saves parameter memory at the cost of higher validation loss.

passages.text: Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present Idea2Prior, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for Idea2Prior, 43.3% for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 36.7% for Gemini web Deep Research under the documented accounting convention. The advantage is concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM; ChatGPT leads on HARD. Selected Idea2Prior runs average 8 minutes 53 seconds, compared with user-reported web averages of 5.2 and 4.7 minutes. A separate nine-query API sample averages $0.0945 per task; this is a historical cost observation, not a matched comparison with web subscription costs. Pairwise Top 5 coverage ranges from 6% to 34%, showing differing returned evidence sets. The system also exposes optional implementation analysis and citation-evolution tools. These results support targeted idea-to-paper retrieval while leaving general web research, forum search, and broader relevance evaluation open.

Researchers often remember an idea before they remember a title: a neighborhood with uncertain boundaries, a circuit transformation with a particular constraint, or an assistant that recognizes when a complex task changes. Recovering relevant prior work from such descriptions is difficult because vocabulary, application setting, and the level of technical detail can differ substantially between a query and a paper. A useful assistant must retrieve candidates, establish their bibliographic identities, and distinguish a close conceptual match from work that merely shares a topic. LLM-based research systems provide useful ways to explore and synthesize sources. STORM organizes research into multi-perspective information gathering and article outlining [ 3 ] , Co-STORM supports interactive exploration [ 4 ] , and Agent Laboratory connects literature review with experimentation and reporting [ 5 ] . Our focus is narrower: given an idea, which five identifiable papers are most likely to match it, and what evidence explains their selection? This objective is not equivalent to the quality of a general research report. We introduce Idea2Prior, an extension of PaperArena and its implementation [ 1 , 2 ] . The contribution is an engineering and evaluation framework for inspectable idea-to-paper retrieval: it preserves search queries, candidate identities, assessments, filtering reasons, PDF availability, and the final ranking. This makes it possible to distinguish a discovery miss from a candidate that was retrieved but lost during filtering, or from a task that failed operationally. A high-level result alone cannot make those distinctions.

The central design separates inexpensive assessment of a broad candidate pool from a bounded examination of document evidence. After abstract assessment and citation expansion, an Expert model jointly considers up to 60 candidates. Five papers are selected for PDF acquisition; unavailable PDFs are not replaced by additional papers in retrieval-only mode. Complete available abstracts remain in the Expert input, along with evidence availability and up to six locally selected PDF passages per acquired paper. A missing PDF does not make a paper irrelevant and does not prevent it from ranking first. The optional full-report mode retains downstream synthesis for users who need a written literature analysis. The revised evaluation covers 30 query cases: ten from each of three prompt tiers, with shared targets across tiers. The reported aggregate Hit@5 is 16/30 for Idea2Prior, 13/30 for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 11/30 for Gemini web Deep Research. The ChatGPT total includes one convention-based credit, disclosed in Section 5.1 . Idea2Prior leads both baselines by 20 percentage points on EASY and MEDIUM, but trails ChatGPT by 10 points on HARD. Mean selected-run latency is 8.89 minutes, and a separately reported nine-query cost sample averages $0.0945. Thus the present evidence shows a recovery advantage in two tiers and a low observed API cost, with longer latency than the supplied browser averages. Our contributions are: 1. An auditable retrieval-and-ranking workflow with identity-aware candidate records, semantic citation filtering, and a joint Top 5 decision over a bounded shortlist.

The released benchmark contains 30 queries in each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD. According to the dataset construction record, GPT-6 Astra in ChatGPT was used to extract and generate the shared literature-search prompts. EASY supplies more identifying detail, MEDIUM removes some detail, and HARD uses shorter, less specific descriptions. These are intended difficulty levels rather than independently calibrated labels. The tiers are not independent paper pools; in particular, MEDIUM and HARD share targets with different wording. The present comparison uses the first ten IDs of each tier: EASY N001–N010, MEDIUM C001–C010, and HARD C001–C010. Each system receives the same filled item prompt: a paper-finding instruction, the 2015–2025 publication/verified-version constraint, up-to-five distinct works with exact bibliographic fields and a short match explanation, identity verification and deduplication requirements, and the idea text. The designated target is not supplied to retrieval. Original prompts and outputs are preserved; Appendix A gives the exact shared wrappers and a three-tier example. These are retrieval prompts, distinct from the internal scoring prompts. ChatGPT and Gemini were tested through their October 2026 web Deep Research interfaces; backend model/build identifiers and subscription tiers were not recorded. Idea2Prior used its API pipeline. Preserved Expert outputs identify the configured alias openai/gemini-3.8-flash ; a compatibility-protocol alias does not independently verify the upstream served model. The released native-Gemini preset is not a newly benchmarked replacement for those historical runs.

Results use final selected runs, including authorized replacements of operationally failed attempts. They therefore measure selected-result recovery, not first-attempt reliability. EASY initially produced five target hits over ten planned queries before recovery; the final selection produced nine. We retain the historical ChatGPT EASY convention of 7/10: six observed hits plus one convention-based counted hit. No returned paper or intersection is fabricated for that credit. Counting only observed hits would make ChatGPT EASY 6/10 and aggregate recovery 12/30; our primary table preserves the earlier agreed convention explicitly. These browser outputs also carry a control limitation: new conversations were used, but the operator reported ChatGPT memory/history references enabled during earlier testing. The adopted HARD comparison uses the replacement NEW report. This historical record does not establish a newly controlled, contamination-free evaluation. Future comparisons should use isolated sessions with memory disabled and a frozen protocol.

passages.text: BRAIn Lab Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights Dmitrii Andriianov 1 , Andrey Veprikov 1,2 , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1,3 1 Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) 2 SB AI Lab 3 Innopolis University Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SpectralWD .

To make the regularizer matrix-aware, we begin with the proximal interpretation of decoupled weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and a 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. At 60 % 60\% label noise, mean clean-test accuracy gains over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization reach 17.78 17.78 points on MNIST and 4.59 4.59 points on four BERT-base tasks.

SliceGPT removes rows and columns after a principal-component transformation [ Ashkboos et al., 2024 ] . ASVD [ Yuan et al., 2023 ] and SVD-LLM [ Wang et al., 2024 ] use activation statistics to improve the factorization. Dobi-SVD learns layerwise truncation and reconstructs weights from truncated activations [ Wang et al., 2025 ] . Prehab fine-tunes a trained model for SVD compression [ Qin et al., 2025 ] . Appendix B.2 compares spectral weight decay with Prehab in this setting. Our main experiments apply it throughout pretraining and evaluate compression and inference with SVD-LLM. Appendix B.4 compares post-training compression methods. Section 3 shows the resulting compression and inference gains.

Figure 5 : Validation loss versus mean effective rank for 124 124 M spectral weight decay pretraining and 32.8 32.8 M-token fine-tuning from an ℓ 2 \ell_{2} WD checkpoint. Pretraining is expensive, motivating methods that prepare existing checkpoints for compression during a short fine-tuning stage. Substantial rank reduction without loss of model quality remains difficult. We compare spectral weight decay during pretraining with its use after pretraining from a standard ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay checkpoint. The 124 124 M-parameter model is pretrained for one Chinchilla-optimal training budget [ Hoffmann et al., 2022 ] , then fine-tuned on 32.8 32.8 M tokens. Figure 5 plots the final validation loss against mean effective rank as the spectral coefficient varies. Within the observed overlap, fine-tuning incurs substantially more loss at the same rank. Fine-tuning also requires a much larger λ \lambda before rank changes appreciably. The sweeps in Figure 5 use λ \lambda values from 0 0 to 7 7 for pretraining and from 4 4 to 250 250 for fine-tuning. Preparing an existing checkpoint for low-rank compression without a substantial loss increase remains open. SLORR also reports difficulties in fine-tuning LLMs with low-rank regularization while preserving their general capabilities [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Appendix B.2 compares spectral weight decay with the fine-tuning method Prehab [ Qin et al., 2025 ] .

We next examine whether the two variants produce different training dynamics with Adam on a 124 124 M-parameter LLaMA trained on FineWeb-Edu at fixed λ = 1 \lambda=1 as the learning rate increases. Figure 10 shows that at η = 0.005 \eta=0.005 , the trajectories nearly coincide, whereas at η = 0.010 \eta=0.010 they separate more clearly. Post-step reaches a lower effective rank but a higher final validation loss at the largest learning rate. This sweep therefore exposes sensitivity to update order, but the accompanying change in rank prevents a clear preference between the variants. Figure 10 : Pre/post-step spectral weight decay with Adam on a 124 124 M-parameter LLaMA trained on FineWeb-Edu at fixed λ = 1 \lambda=1 . The top row shows validation loss after 1.5 1.5 B tokens, and the bottom row shows mean effective rank from the start of training. Dashed curves denote pre-step and solid curves post-step. Our LLM pretraining experiments show little difference between the two update orders at small learning rates. The synthetic recovery tasks favor post-step on average, with generally modest gains. Both schemes have the same computational requirements, so we adopt post-step and recommend it as the default.

We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and a 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. SliceGPT removes rows and columns after a principal-component transformation [ Ashkboos et al., 2024 ] . ASVD [ Yuan et al., 2023 ] and SVD-LLM [ Wang et al., 2024 ] use activation statistics to improve the factorization. Dobi-SVD learns layerwise truncation and reconstructs weights from truncated activations [ Wang et al., 2025 ] . Prehab fine-tunes a trained model for SVD compression [ Qin et al., 2025 ] . Appendix B.2 compares spectral weight decay with Prehab in this setting. Our main experiments apply it throughout pretraining and evaluate compression and inference with SVD-LLM. Appendix B.4 compares post-training compression methods. Section 3 shows the resulting compression and inference gains.

The 124 124 M-parameter model is pretrained for one Chinchilla-optimal training budget [ Hoffmann et al., 2022 ] , then fine-tuned on 32.8 32.8 M tokens. Figure 5 plots the final validation loss against mean effective rank as the spectral coefficient varies. Within the observed overlap, fine-tuning incurs substantially more loss at the same rank. Preparing an existing checkpoint for low-rank compression without a substantial loss increase remains open. 2610.10965:b347fff04eab5d040cc0edd461ba7.question: On NanoGPT, how do Spectrally Targeted Muon variants compare with standard Muon in training loss or speed, and what do the measured weight effective-rank changes show?

passages.text: The Muon optimizer orthogonalizes each update matrix, setting all of its singular values to one, and has proven highly effective for training large language models. It remains unclear, however, whether this success comes from amplifying small singular directions that gradient descent neglects or from suppressing large, degenerate directions that disrupt training. We introduce Spectrally Targeted Muon, which orthogonalizes only the singular values above or below a threshold τ \tau , so that varying τ \tau interpolates between normalized SGD and Muon. It isolates the relevant singular subspaces with projections computed by Newton-Schulz iteration on a shifted Gram matrix, so no SVD is needed. We evaluate these variants on the CIFAR-10 and NanoGPT speedruns, tracking the effective rank of gradient, update, and weight matrices and a new metric, the alignment of updates with the tangent space of the weight matrix’s isospectral manifold. We find three things. First, the small singular values of the momentum are not noise. Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix nearly matches Muon while touching only a small fraction of the momentum, whereas orthogonalizing only the top falls well short even though it holds almost all of it. On language models every momentum singular value is far below one, so targeted orthogonalization can only amplify, and Muon wins by making directions that are too small to train on at their raw scale trainable. Second, shrinking the largest singular values is what keeps the parameter spectrum flat; this is cheap, and it is not what drives the loss. Third, AdamW differs from Muon mainly in how slowly it builds structure, which explains its slower start and why warmup helps AdamW but only hurts Muon.

The Muon optimizer for deep learning works by orthogonalizing the update matrix ( Jordan et al., 2024b ) . Unlike many other proposed optimizers, this has been highly successful empirically for training large language models, especially when coupled with weight decay ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . This is because the matrix can be orthogonalized relatively efficiently, using methods such as Newton-Schulz or Polar Express ( Amsel et al., 2026 ) . The orthogonalization step can be thought of as applying the matrix sign function to the gradient matrix, which normalizes all the singular values to one, prompting the question of whether Muon’s success comes from amplifying small but important directions with small singular values ignored by standard gradient descent, or from normalizing large, degenerate directions with large singular values that misdirect the training. In this paper, we will explore a method to target this orthogonalization to singular values either above or below a certain threshold τ \tau , and we will also experiment with different values for this threshold, thus allowing us to interpolate between SGD and Muon with a spectrally targeted version. Specifically, we will apply these Muon variants to the two speedrun tasks originally used to show Muon’s performance, the CIFAR-10 dataset with a convolutional network, and the NanoGPT large language model, just as in Jordan et al. (2024b) . In addition to standard performance metrics, we will examine other metrics more pertinent to the linear-algebraic structure of our weight and update matrices. This allows us to explore what characteristics of matrix optimizers lead to richer learning.

Figure 4: Effective rank of the gradient (a) and update (b), averaged over all matrices, and of the value (c), attention-output (d) and MLP (e) parameters, averaged over layers (seed 0). Dashed lines are the warmup variants, the dotted line in (a) marks the start of the learning rate cooldown, and the legend in (b) applies to all panels. We use the effective rank of the gradient and update matrix to help explain our optimizer performances. Since the gradient depends only on the surrounding loss landscape and not the optimizer, it tells us which optimizers enter parts of the loss landscape where many directions are available. This happens quickly for Muon and the targeted variants, while AdamW takes a few hundred steps to get there. During learning rate cooldown, this effective rank grows for every optimizer, because the leading singular values of the gradient shrink while its bulk stays put. In the river-valley picture of Wen et al. (2024) , the component of the gradient along the sharp valley walls dies with the learning rate while the component along the flat floor remains. Gradient rank thus tells us where the iterate sits in the valley, bouncing between the walls or settled on the floor. Meanwhile, the effective rank of the update shows the difference between the different types of targeting, with bottom targeting creating an update shaped like Muon’s, while top targeting creates an even lower rank update than AdamW. (a) Log-barrier of the isospectral tangent fraction, averaged over matrices; the grey dotted line is the value for a random rotation, the orange dotted line marks the start of the learning rate cooldown, and dashed lines are the warmup variants. (b) Share of the spectrum-changing part of the update at each singular direction of the parameter, ranked by singular value, averaged over matrices and steps 100–1500; the dotted line is uniform. (c) Final validation loss against final parameter effective rank, including the learning rate controls; the bottom-targeted runs at τ ≤ 4 × 10 − 4 \tau\leq 4\times 10^{-4} leave their MLP output matrices barely trained. Next, we examined the parameter effective ranks across different types of Transformer parameters in Figure 4 (c)–(e). We were able to observe the same results as Wang et al. (2025) , who found that AdamW heavily reduces the effective rank of parameters, unlike Muon, giving Muon a richer associative memory and better performance on tail classes. However, top targeted variants fall the most, and their zero-initialized output projections never gain much rank at all. This implies that the rich learning is a direct consequence of participation by the small singular values.

The parameter effective rank depends on the part of the update that changes the spectrum, meaning the part aligned with the parameter’s own singular basis, and how concentrated it is in the leading directions of this basis. Figure 5 (b) shows this directly: the top targeted and AdamW curves peak at the leading directions, while Muon and the bottom arm stay near uniform. Intuitively, an update that keeps pushing along the leading singular directions of a matrix reinforces what is already there, while a full-spectrum update mostly rotates the basis and leaves the spectrum unchanged. Figure 5 (c) plots these against the final loss. Figure 5 (a) shows the same thing with the isospectral tangent metric of Section 3.3 . Every optimizer puts more of its update into the parameter’s own basis than a random update would, and tangent alignment rises for every optimizer over training, fastest during the cooldown. Among the targeted variants of Muon, the bottom targeted versions show higher alignment than Muon, while the top targeted versions show lower alignment. This is reversed compared to the CIFAR experiments, but it reveals the same underlying phenomenon. In the NanoGPT domain, the targeted region has its magnitude raised, while the remaining regions are relatively suppressed. Therefore, it is simply the top few directions of the gradient which lie within the existing basis of the parameter, and the more you shrink them in the update, the less poorly conditioned the parameter matrices become. Note that structure and performance don’t move together: AdamW collapses rank and still performs well, the bottom targeted variants keep Muon’s rank without matching its loss, and full-spectrum updates keep the spectrum flat for free. 2611.17191:9d1924e75cb113e64dbaee2a8256f.question: In language-model LoRA rank sweeps, how does Rényi-2 effective-rank regularization compare with standard LoRA on held-out perplexity, forgetting, and training cost at matched rank, training budget, and tuned hyperparameters?

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning–forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one model–rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning–forgetting frontier. Our code is available at

Concretely, we study regularized training objectives that augment the standard language-modeling loss L L with a capacity regularization term that focuses on maximizing the effective rank. Direct spectral differentiation requires care at rank-deficient updates and incurs SVD overhead (Appendix D .1). We therefore use an SVD-free surrogate, the Rényi-2 effective rank erank 2 ​ ( Δ ​ W ) \mathrm{erank}_{2}(\Delta W) . We develop two approaches to increasing this effective-rank surrogate. First, norm-bounded capacity maximization couples a Roy–Vetterli lower bound with Norm-Bounded LoRA (NB-LoRA) Wang et al. (2025) : by enforcing an operator-norm cap and maximizing the Frobenius norm within that cap, one can raise effective rank through a principled constrained reparameterization. This strategy works in practice but limits the adapter weight updates to a specialized parameterization which often results in unstable training empirically. Therefore, we propose a simpler, differentiable, parameterization-agnostic and easy-to-optimize regularization strategy called the Rényi-2 penalty as our main method, which directly maximizes erank 2 ​ ( Δ ​ W ) \mathrm{erank}_{2}(\Delta W) . This penalty is not only applicable to vanilla LoRA, but also to improved spectral variants such as PiSSA Meng et al. (2025) and LoRA-XS Bałazy et al. (2025) .

Standard LoRA training often underutilizes its allocated subspace so nominal rank is an unreliable proxy for usable adapter capacity in the learning–forgetting trade-off. We proposed effective-rank maximization via the Rényi-2 penalty, a parameterization-agnostic, SVD-free term added to the language-modeling loss, and showed across mixed-domain SFT, task-specific SFT, rank sweeps, and scheduling ablations that it can reduce forgetting on pretraining proxies while maintaining competitive target-task fit. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models, λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA, with mean Train PPL improving or increasing by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one comparison. Our single-task and scheduling experiments also demonstrate configuration-dependent learning and retention outcomes: the penalty can improve retention without a large training-fit cost, but does not eliminate the learning–forgetting trade-off. Spectral diagnostics provide descriptive comparisons of the resulting updates. Effective rank is therefore not merely a post-hoc diagnostic but a trainable objective that regularizes toward fuller utilization.

Unless a table caption states otherwise, all numbers are taken from the terminal training state of a completed run; we do not reload an in-run best-validation checkpoint. Early stopping is disabled. Periodic evals run every 100 100 optimizer steps; perplexity and forgetting probes below are the values logged at the last eval before the run hits its token or epoch budget. Train PPL is exp ⁡ ( H ) \exp(H) where H H is an exponential moving average ( β = 0.99 \beta{=}0.99 ) of the assistant-only training loss; it is a smoothed training-loss proxy, not held-out validation perplexity. Wiki PPL and StarCoder PPL are reference-probe perplexities on fixed OLMo-Mix-1124 slices, using the plain-text supervision protocol and batch limits specified above. In the mixed-domain setting we additionally log in-mixture retention probes on held-out GSM8K and WMT19 Czech–English validation text; Appendix Table 5 reports both in-mixture probes. eRank is the Roy–Vetterli effective rank of the accumulated adapter update Δ ​ W \Delta W , averaged over all targeted down_proj modules, taken from the last logged rank diagnostic. This is distinct from the Rényi-2 surrogate used in the objective. Dense down-projection fine-tuning baselines select hyperparameters via a separate sweep (Section F.1 ), but reported metrics still refer to the terminal state of the selected run. Post-hoc spectral analyses (intruder dimensions, subspace alignment, singular-direction mixing) use measurements from the final saved checkpoint.

passages.section: G.2 Mixed-domain rank and penalty sensitivity
passages.text: These sweeps examine how the learning–retention balance changes with the configured rank and penalty weight. Fuller spectral utilization need not improve every perplexity metric, so effective rank should be interpreted jointly with mixture fit and the held-out probes.

Spectral diagnostics provide descriptive comparisons of the resulting updates. Effective rank is therefore not merely a post-hoc diagnostic but a trainable objective that regularizes toward fuller utilization.

2610.04249:8fbd1835323a843ec9b0d39201868.question: What balance and alignment assumptions underlie the singular-mode results, and what language-model experiments, if any, test the predicted differences among GD, Muon, Shampoo, and Adam in weight effective rank and validation loss?

passages.text: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

passages.section: Implicit bias of Adam and related adaptive methods.
passages.text: Cattaneo et al. (2023) use backward error analysis to characterize corrections to Adam and RMSProp dynamics, relating implicit regularization to hyperparameters and training stage. The classification literature builds on the maximum margin characterization of GD for separable data ( Soudry et al., 2018 ) . Wang et al. (2021) study limiting parameter directions in homogeneous classification under their adaptive flow assumptions. Zhang et al. (2024) establish a maximum ℓ ∞ \ell_{\infty} margin result for full batch Adam in separable linear classification. Xie and Li (2024) connect AdamW, which includes decoupled weight decay, to ℓ ∞ \ell_{\infty} -norm constrained optimization under full-batch assumptions. Vasudeva et al. (2026) analyze a difference in feature learning between Adam and GD in a Gaussian classification model with two layer ReLU networks. These results concern distinct losses, optimizer conventions, or notions of bias. Our squared loss analysis studies finite singular amplitudes and phase times without weight decay, so classification margin results do not directly determine its birth or saturation laws.

We first evaluate the optimizer dependent spectral dynamics in the full observation matrix factorization setting described in App. F , where the theoretical phase laws apply most directly. Figure 4: Optimizer geometry sets the pace of spectral learning evaluation in matrix factorization. (a) Evolution of a weak target mode with μ = 0.18 \mu=0.18 , shown as the learned fraction σ ⁡ ( t ) / μ \sigma(t)/\mu . GD exhibits the factorization induced small mode barrier, whereas normalization and preconditioning substantially accelerate emergence. (b) Birth time to the common amplitude b = 0.03 b=0.03 as the target mode μ \mu varies. While ideal Muon is independent of the target mode ordering during birth, other optimizers are target sensitive. (c) Decay trajectories for an unsupported mode with target μ = 0 \mu=0 . Ideal Muon removes the mode in finite time, undamped K-FAC produces exponential decay, while GD, instantaneous Adam with fixed stabilization, and cumulative Shampoo retain increasingly slow tails near zero. Optimizer geometry therefore determines which spectral components emerge, persist, and disappear.

Fig. 4 provides a broader validation of the theory in addition to the theoretical evaluation done in Sec. 6 . Fig. 5 compares the optimization and rank dynamics. Although the methods eventually reach similar losses and effective ranks, their trajectories differ substantially. GD learns the target modes sequentially and retains a low effective rank for longer, consistent with the small mode mobility factor σ p \sigma^{p} . Adam reduces this separation and activates weaker modes much earlier. Muon produces an even more rapid redistribution of spectral mass, reflecting its normalized spectral update. Cumulative Shampoo initially behaves more like GD but quickly changes regime as its accumulated preconditioner adapts. K-FAC exhibits a smoother evolution in which curvature correction reduces the factorization induced separation between mode time scales. The stable and effective rank curves therefore mainly differ during the transient phase, while their later agreement reflects the unique full observation target rather than identical optimization dynamics. Figure 5: Optimization and rank dynamics in matrix factorization. All optimizers train the same depth L = 4 L=4 deep linear factorization toward the same rank eight target and reach comparable final training loss. Left: training loss over optimization steps. Middle: stable rank of W W . Right: effective rank of W W . The optimizers exhibit markedly different transient rank dynamics despite converging toward similar final spectra. GD retains a lower rank representation for longer, whereas Adam, Muon, cumulative Shampoo, and K-FAC alter the rate at which spectral mass is distributed across modes.

We next consider a less structured setting in which the effective predictor is trained by underdetermined linear regression as described in App. F . This experiment tests whether the qualitative predictions persist once our simplifying assumptions Assumptions 1 , 2 and 3 are removed. Fig. 16 shows that the optimizers reach comparable training losses and converge to nearly identical final singular spectra. This agreement is important: the pronounced differences observed during training are not simply consequences of one method converging to a substantially different level of fit. Nevertheless, the stable and effective ranks evolve differently. Thus similar terminal predictors need not imply similar spectral learning dynamics. Figure 16: Optimizer dependent dynamics persist in underdetermined linear regression. We train the same deep linear predictor on an underdetermined, nonwhitened regression problem using GD, Adam, Muon, cumulative Shampoo, and KFAC. All methods reach comparable final loss and final spectra of W W despite substantially different transient dynamics shown by the stable rank and effective rank throughout training. The optimizer geometry strongly changes how quickly spectral mass concentrates.

The singular value trajectories in Fig. 17 make this distinction particularly clear. GD exhibits pronounced separation between the emergence times of successive singular values, consistent with the factorization induced small mode barrier derived in the aligned setting. Adam substantially compresses these delays. Muon produces a markedly more synchronized growth of the singular spectrum, consistent with normalization reducing mode dependent mobility differences. Cumulative Shampoo also accelerates weaker spectral components after its preconditioner has accumulated sufficient history, while K-FAC produces comparatively smooth growth across the spectrum through curvature correction. These effects remain visible even though the singular vectors are not fixed and the data covariance couples the modes. The experiment therefore supports the interpretation of the theoretical phase laws as mechanisms governing transient spectral learning rather than merely properties of the special aligned model. Exact exponents depend on the aligned reduction, but the resulting qualitative distinctions persist in the more practical underdetermined regression problem. (a) GD (b) Adam (c) Muon (d) Shampoo (e) K-FAC Figure 17: Singular value trajectories in nonaligned underdetermined linear regression. Although all methods approach similar final singular spectra, their transient spectrum differ substantially. The qualitative optimizer dependent dynamics predicted by the aligned phase analysis remain visible even when the empirical data covariance couples singular directions and the exact scalar mode reduction no longer holds.

passages.text: Building on this framework, we propose NormPre, a family of matrix optimizers comprising NormPre-G and NormPre-L, which realize marginal normalization followed by global and localized spectral preconditioning, respectively. Both variants combine relaxed tangent momentum processing with alternating row/column normalization and consistent update RMS scaling. Specifically, NormPre-G approximates the full-spectrum transformation via Newton-Schulz iterations. For NormPre-L, the leading interaction eigenspace is obtained through exact extraction or scalable randomized sketching. We also establish 𝒪 ( T − 1 / 2 ) \mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2}) convergence guarantees for simplified NormPre-G and exact NormPre-L, extending them to sketch-based NormPre-L under controlled approximation error. Empirically, our extensive pretraining evaluations span GPT-2 Small on OpenWebText, LLaMA models up to 1.3B on C4, and Qwen3 models up to 1.7B on Pile. Under matched training budgets, both variants consistently outperform established baselines that represent distinct optimization paradigms: coordinate-wise adaptation (AdamW), matrix orthogonalization (Muon), and normalization (MANO). Furthermore, our spectral dynamics and efficiency analyses highlight that NormPre-L with localized preconditioning delivers strong optimization gains at lower cost and NormPre-G with global preconditioning further reduces validation loss, providing practitioners with flexible choices to balance optimization performance and computational cost. Figure 2: Geometric Workflow of the NormPre Optimizer (Algorithm 1 ). Our main contributions are summarized as follows.

Experimental Setup. We evaluate NormPre across model scales, architectures and datasets. Our experiments cover GPT-2 Small on OpenWebText ( Radford et al., 2019 ; Gokaslan and Cohen, 2019 ) , LLaMA-{130M, 350M, 1.3B} on C4 ( Touvron et al., 2023 ; Raffel et al., 2020 ) , and Qwen3-{0.6B, 1.7B} on Pile ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2020 ) . We compare NormPre-G and NormPre-L with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) and MANO ( Gu and Xie, 2026 ) . NormPre-G uses five Newton-Schulz iterations and NormPre-L uses the Sketch implementation with rank r = 32 r=32 . All models are trained for 10,000 10{,}000 steps with a sequence length of 1024 1024 and an effective batch size of 512 512 . Within each setting, all optimizers use matched model initialization, data order, training budget and evaluation protocol. Detailed configurations are provided in Appendix A.1 . 2610.04507:8d15476f53c3c798fd8f5cd24017e.question: In the 7B language-model label-noise experiment, how do LoRA rank, noisy-label memorization, clean held-out performance, and parameter cost compare with module-matched dense fine-tuning? What controls and seeds support the comparison?

passages.text: Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter’s rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. On DeiT-Tiny, risk is lowest at rank one and rises sharply as the adapter becomes able to fit the noisy labels, forming an interpolation cliff. Past the peak, risk falls again, but every tested post-peak rank that still saves parameters remains above dense risk. Rank-one LoRA outperforms dense fine-tuning on three of the four vision backbones, consistent with strong regularization at small rank. LoRA thus exhibits a second descent, but matches dense risk only after losing its parameter advantage, first on DeiT-Tiny at four times dense’s projection weights. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/lora-second-descent-C7B5 .

Double descent. The risk peak at interpolation and its subsequent descent were established by Belkin et al. (2019) , Spigler et al. (2019) and Advani et al. (2020) , extended to deep networks, epochs and data by Nakkiran et al. (2020) , and analyzed precisely in linear and random-features models ( Hastie et al., 2022 ; Mei & Montanari, 2022 ; Bartlett et al., 2020 ) , as reviewed by Belkin (2021) . Label noise amplifies the peak ( Nakkiran et al., 2020 ) , regularization can suppress it ( Nakkiran et al., 2021 ) , and related structure includes triple descent ( d’Ascoli et al., 2020 ) and grokking ( Power et al., 2022 ; Davies et al., 2023 ) . Nearest to our phenomenon, Xue et al. (2024) report a “final ascent” in the widest models once the noise-to-sample ratio is large, a regime our from-scratch transformer reproduces and our ResNet controls do not (Section 5.6 ). Closest in spirit to our diagnosis, Curth et al. (2023) argue that double descent hinges on what the capacity axis measures and Schaeffer et al. (2023) isolate the ingredients producing the peak. In transfer learning, Dar & Baraniuk (2022) analyze linear transfer and Dar et al. (2022) sweep frozen-layer count, neither along adapter rank.

LoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) builds on intrinsic-dimension measurements of objective landscapes ( Li et al., 2018 ; Aghajanyan et al., 2021 ) ; its rank expressivity is characterized by Zeng & Lee (2024) and its scaling conventions by Kalajdzievski (2023) . That large ranks can hurt is established: accuracy stagnates past ranks of 32 32 – 64 64 ( Jung et al., 2025 ) , optima are task-dependent ( Rathore et al., 2025 ) , LoRA “learns less and forgets less” ( Biderman et al., 2024 ) , and low-rank updates memorize less in large language models ( Bossy et al., 2026 ) ; in noisy-label classification, Kim et al. (2024) find that the capacity limit of PEFT also impedes learning clean examples. Under label noise, theory places the optimal rank lower as noise grows ( Steele, 2026 ) and accuracy degrades with rank when noise is strong ( Zindari et al., 2026 ) , while Park (2026) and Rushka & Klabjan (2026) analyze rank sufficiency and approximation error. Empirically, Dennis et al. (2026) find ranks 16 16 to 128 128 all trailing full fine-tuning and Albert et al. (2025) ask whether the shortfall is parameters or rank, neither under label noise. These establish the two endpoints. What remains unmeasured is the shape between them, where risk peaks relative to the rank at which optimization interpolates, and whether the post-peak branch recovers once the adapter can express any dense update.

Effective capacity and optimization geometry. That LoRA’s update carries a stable rank well below its nominal rank is likewise established, as a pathology to engineer away ( Lion et al., 2025 ) and as a sweep locating where validation accuracy turns ( Awofeso et al., 2025 ) ; we add its placement relative to interpolation and an intervention on it. Parameterization matters beyond expressivity ( Shuttleworth et al., 2025 ) , and learning rate interacts with rank through initialization and scaling ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , which is why the shared-rate sweep is checked against per-arm rates (each at its own rate) on every backbone (Section 5.3 , Appendices C.2 and C.3 ). The optimization geometry of the factored parameterization is mapped: freezing one factor ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Zhu et al., 2024 ) or both ( Kopiczko et al., 2024 ) , preconditioning the gradient ( Zhang & Pilanci, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Ghosh et al., 2026 ) , and showing that different factorizations of one Δ ​ W \Delta W converge differently ( Castin et al., 2026 ; Oh et al., 2026 ) . Those results concern training and generalization of the factorization; ours concern where the post-peak branch reaches dense risk (Section 5.3 ). Chang et al. (2025) use “double descent” for a transient training-loss divergence, a different object. Memorization and calibration under noise. Interpolating noisy labels forces memorization ( Zhang et al., 2017 ; Feldman & Zhang, 2020 ) , and calibration itself depends on overparameterization in high-dimensional models ( Clarté et al., 2023 ) , which is why we separate the risk we measure from the temperature it is read at (Section 5.6 ).

Model selection shrinks the cliff without removing it. Selecting learning rate, weight decay and stopping epoch on a clean validation split reduces the cliff from 0.53 0.53 to 0.16 0.16 nats. The selected models retain the rank ordering on fresh seeds, and every selected checkpoint precedes interpolation (Appendix E.2 ), which is the mechanism: selection escapes the cliff by declining to interpolate, not by crossing it. Because per-rank selection includes no dense arm, it bears on the shape of the axis and not on the gap to dense. No tested setting removes the cliff once ranks interpolate. Corrupting the frozen backbone only deepens the cliff, and its shape persists through changes in data size, learning rate, weight decay, scaling, adapter placement and dataset (Appendices C.2 , E.1 and E.3 ; Table 15 ). Architecture decides too. A ResNet completes the descent on these subsets; a width-scaled ViT trained from scratch does not (Appendix B.2 ), recovering 0.56 0.56 of 3.23 3.23 nats, the final-ascent regime of Xue et al. (2024) . Dense-block fine-tuning of a transformer reaches Rec = 0.82 \mathrm{Rec}{=}0.82 , so the rank axis’s shallow far side is not a transformer property. Scope. The experiments cover noisy image and text classification with AdamW, synthetic and human label noise, and budgets up to 160 160 epochs. The dense reference is module-matched, training the projections LoRA adapts rather than the whole network; the dense-block axis of Section 5.5 unfreezes up to six full blocks. Test NLL is the primary measurement, and accuracy follows its ordering inside the parameter-saving window but can diverge at larger ranks. Where LoRA crosses dense depends on the protocol and the grid.

The rank axis does run a second descent, and a sweep that stops at full rank can miss it. Judging what this descent is worth requires a reference point, which the module-matched rank sweep supplies by grading every setting against dense fine-tuning of the identical modules with the trainable-parameter ratio beside it. Across four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model, no measured post-peak rank that still saves parameters reaches dense, and the first equivalence result sits at four times dense’s projection weights under a single shared learning rate. Full rank supplies the expressivity, so the remaining gap is a matter of coordinates, which the frozen-factor interventions show can move risk by about the size of the gap. LoRA’s parameter advantage is strongest at the cheap end and runs out in the tail; rank-one LoRA dominates dense outright on three of the four vision backbones. Rank keeps shaping generalization long after it stops saving parameters.
