2611.07859:0fbf0c3ddbd8e1926f98d90de921b.question: In CORE's closed-search experiments, what answer-accuracy and evidence-recall gains does it achieve over Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher, and what ablations isolate snippet selection and context management at matched search and token budgets?

passages.text: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE , a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

The key idea of our CORE, a co arse-to-fine deep re search harness, is to shift this burden from the agent to the search itself: relevant text is found by searching over broad passages, while the agent receives only concise snippets. We organize the search space into documents, passages, segments, and snippets, and treat evidence as the text admitted into the agent’s context to serve the local goal of a sub-query or the global goal of the question. CORE’s search tool first performs coarse retrieval of passages with a reasoning-aware dense retriever ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , then fine-grained reranking with a late-interaction model ( Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Chaffin, 2025 ) , whose token-level similarities also locate the most relevant snippet within each passage at no additional encoding cost. CORE’s context manager lets the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources and deduplicates snippets across searches. Our contributions are as follows: • Coarse-to-fine search. CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level. It reuses the token-level similarities computed during late-interaction reranking to locate the most relevant snippet in each passage, without any additional encoding. • A training-free harness. CORE combines coarse-to-fine search with context management and works with any agent model without retraining. Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

• State-of-the-art closed-search results at scale. Under controlled settings, we compare CORE with two recent state-of-the-art open-source harnesses, Tongyi DeepResearch ( Tongyi DeepResearch Team et al., 2025 ) and OpenResearcher ( Li et al., 2026b ) , on BrowseComp-Plus ( Chen et al., 2026c ) , BrowseComp-Wikipedia ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and BrowseComp-Plus CM ( Sharifymoghaddam et al., 2026 ) . To ensure reproducibility, we restrict the study to closed search over fixed corpora. Across three agent models, CORE achieves the highest accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark comparison, setting new state-of-the-art results to the best of our knowledge.

CORE achieves the highest answer accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark group, producing new state-of-the-art results. On BrowseComp-Plus, it improves both metrics over the stronger baseline, OpenResearcher, for all three agent models. The gains are largest for Qwen3.8-27B, at 6.39 points in accuracy and 7.40 points in recall. On BrowseComp-Wikipedia, CORE keeps its lead across all three agents. With GPT-5.4, it improves both metrics by more than eight points over OpenResearcher. Higher accuracy therefore comes with broader coverage of the annotated relevant documents in both the web and Wikipedia corpora. See some case studies in Appendix C .

We presented CORE , a training-free deep research harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves whole passages to judge relevance, then reuses the reranker’s token-level similarities to return only the most relevant snippet from each one. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. Across three agent models and three benchmarks, CORE achieves higher answer accuracy and evidence recall than Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher in every model–benchmark comparison, while returning substantially fewer tokens per search than Tongyi DeepResearch. These results show that deep research agents can answer more accurately from shorter search responses when relevant text is selected before it enters their context.

passages.text: We compare Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B and OpenResearcher-30B-A3B ( Li et al., 2026b ) under CORE on BrowseComp-Plus. Both use the same corpus, passage index, retrieval and context-management configuration, and GPT-5.5 judge at high reasoning effort. Sampling parameters follow Appendix A.2 ; context budgets and tool-call formats follow each model’s configuration. Table 3 shows higher answer accuracy for Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B in this setting, supporting its selection for the main experiments. Trace-norm regularization then forces the optimizer to pick a low-rank matrix among all matrices that produce the same observed output. This yields global minimizers whose ranks are controlled by the rank of this map, which we call the bottleneck rank , rather than the sample size. For multi-head attention, we obtain tighter rank upper bounds by exploiting two additional invariances: row-wise softmax is insensitive to additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. For the factorized LoRA objective with weight decay, we prove a complementary result on the nonconvex side: after an arbitrarily small generic positive semidefinite perturbation, every first-order stationary point is rank-deficient once the LoRA rank exceeds a threshold determined by the bottleneck rank. Finally, we show that global minimizers of the perturbed objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm problem, and we provide uniform generalization bounds governed by the spectral structure of the frozen features. 0 0 footnotetext: ⋆ Corresponding author.

(2025) analyze fine-tuning through linearization under an explicit ℓ 2 \ell_{2} bias toward the pretrained model. Beyond classical linearization, Kim et al. Finally, we show that global minimizers of the perturbed objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm problem, and we provide uniform generalization bounds governed by the spectral structure of the frozen features. 0 0 footnotetext: ⋆ Corresponding author.

Fine-tuning large pretrained models on downstream tasks is effective but expensive: updating all parameters of a billion-scale model requires substantial memory and compute. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) solves this problem by adapting a large pretrained model while updating only a small subset of parameters. Some of the representative approaches include adapter modules ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , prefix tuning ( Li and Liang, 2021 ) , prompt tuning, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022 ). Among these, LoRA stands out as an attractive option because it keeps the pretrained backbone frozen and modifies selected linear maps by adding trainable low-rank updates. More formally, for a weight matrix W 0 ∈ ℝ m × n W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , LoRA parameterizes the adapted weight as W = W 0 + T , T = U ​ V ⊤ , U ∈ ℝ m × r , V ∈ ℝ n × r , W=W_{0}+T,\qquad T=UV^{\top},\qquad U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, The rank r r is typically chosen by the practitioner as a hyperparameter rather than something derived from the fine-tuning objective itself ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Schulman and Lab, 2025 ) . A fundamental theoretical question is therefore: When does the regularized fine-tuning objective itself admit a low-rank global minimizer, and what controls the rank?

Most existing theory addresses nearby questions through linearization or simplified training dynamics. In the NTK regime, Jang et al. (2024) shows that full fine-tuning admits a low-rank solution and that sufficiently overparameterized LoRA eliminates spurious local minima. Afzal et al. (2025) analyze fine-tuning through linearization under an explicit ℓ 2 \ell_{2} bias toward the pretrained model. Beyond classical linearization, Kim et al. (2025) study LoRA dynamics and prove a dichotomy between convergence to a low-rank global minimizer and convergence to a qualitatively different high-rank solution. These works are complementary to ours, but they do not answer a more structural question: what property of the objective function makes low-rank optima available in the first place?

Our answer starts with a simple observation: once the backbone is frozen, the loss does not observe an adapted matrix T T directly, but only through a finite-rank linear map determined by the frozen activations. Concretely, if H = [ h 1 , … , h N ] H=[h_{1},\ldots,h_{N}] is the matrix of frozen input features across the N N training samples, the empirical loss depends on T T only through the product T ​ H TH . We call rank ⁡ ( Φ ) \rank(\Phi) , where Φ ⁡ ( T ) = T ​ H \Phi(T)=TH , the bottleneck rank of the adapted block. The same principle applies blockwise to multiple adapted stages and attention heads. Trace-norm regularization then selects a low-rank representative among all matrices that induce the same observed output. This yields exact low-rank existence results without linearizing the network around the pretrained weights. For multi-head attention ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) , the same principle becomes sharper because attention introduces additional invariances: row-wise softmax is unchanged by additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and the frozen output projection.
